selected.headline: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? | Explainer News
selected.evidence: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive. Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”. He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”. “The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera. Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts. “Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said. “The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.” Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city. In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force. Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi. It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting. Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement. That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorate

selected.headline: Saudis probe how defense systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
selected.evidence: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Fears of intensifying conflict were growing in Saudi Arabia on Monday after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched multiple strikes on Riyadh’s airport over the weekend, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. “What is clear is we remain on a strong escalation ladder,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region. More than 300 people were injured when the kingdom’s main international airport was attacked Saturday, marking a major escalation in the Houthi rebel group’s campaign against the world’s leading oil exporter and key U.S. ally in the region. Among the victims were one American, as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese national. The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia later said that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died. Video capturing the Saturday attack showed a packed airport before the flash of an explosion sends people running for safety as debris falls on them. The airport remained shut Monday. The impact of the attacks were felt at the WPC Energy Congress in the Saudi capital Monday, with several top energy executives dropping off the event’s schedule. The chief executives of Exxon Mobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which started Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organizers released early Monday, Reuters reported. The energy giants did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News. “You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said, according to Reuters, as he opened Monday’s session of the gathering held just miles away from Riyadh airport. But, he added, “our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.” He said the stepped-up fighting was serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious.” “There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix,” he separately said. “We come out of the ashes all the time and every time.” Fighting on the ground in neighboring Yemen is also intensifying, with the Houthis expanding their operations along its Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb, a key shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 after the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. A period of relative calm following a 2022 ceasefire was shattered in July when the Houthis resumed attacks after accusing Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was attempting to land. Baron said the latest attacks — the deadliest by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade — could have a “galvanizing effect” on Washington and other international actors, including Pakistan and Turkey, which recently reached a joint defense agreement with the kingdom. “As these attacks are growing stronger and stronger, on the one hand, it’s increasing the hurt on the kingdom, but it’s also increasing assessments for many that there has to be some strong effort to degrade the Houthis and restore deterrence,” Baron said. Washington faces mounting pressure. President Donald Trump on Saturday said he was still weighing whether to join in Saudi Arabia’s military operations against the Houthis. “We may. We’re gonna look at it,” he told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.” After sweeping gains by Houthi forces in Yemen last month, Trump said the rebel group had contacted the U.S. to stress that it doesn’t “want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.” While the skies over Riyadh were empty Monday after flights in and out of the capital were canceled, roads were full of traffic as residents tried to get back to normal life. And in the early hours of Sunday, road crossings at the border with the United Arab Emirates were largely deserted. “With the Houthis, we knew that they could hit Riyadh airport, but it’s almost about the precision,” Baron said. “There’s a great degree of anxiety in terms of ... living in a world where you can just have random armed groups hitting airports.”

selected.headline: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
selected.evidence: Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities". There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country. He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities." "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added. Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday. On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks. Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said. Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire". On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district. Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured. Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine? When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday , Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire". For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure , disrupting energy supplies on both sides. Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter. In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025. Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year. Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. However, there has been a mixed response among European officials. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it." Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working". selected.headline: Joint statement: States Must Act Now to Protect the International Criminal Court from Unlawful US Sanctions | ICJ
selected.evidence: Donate to the ICJ By donating to the ICJ, you are actively participating in creating a just society. I want to help 12 Oct 2026 | Advocacy , Joint Statement , News The Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CICC), the more than 120 undersigned organisations from over 60 countries representing all regions, and dozens of legal experts, human rights defenders and members of the European Parliament, condemn unequivocally and in the strongest terms the decision by co the United States (US) to impose unlawful sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). This unprecedented measure represents a direct attack against the rule of law, the independence of the Court and international justice, ultimately undermining the rights of millions of victims and survivors of mass atrocities worldwide. The ICC has shown remarkable resilience in steadfastly discharging its mandate in the face of escalating attacks. Now, States Parties must match this commitment by defending the Court they themselves established and protecting those who cooperate with it. Condemnations alone are not enough; coordinated action is urgently needed to protect the Court’s ability to function. On 9 October 2026, the US announced the imposition of sanctions against the ICC as an institution under Executive Order 14203 . These sanctions mark the gravest escalation in the sustained campaign carried out by the US with the declared aim of dismantling the ICC “brick by brick” for having investigated crimes allegedly committed on the territory of a State Party by US nationals or their allies, in particular Israeli nationals . Under the Rome Statute, the Court may exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed on the territory of a State Party, irrespective of the nationality of the alleged perpetrator. Since February 2025, the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the former ICC Prosecutor, Karim Khan ; both Deputy Prosecutors ; the ICC President and eight other judges; a staff member and judicial candidate ; a UN Special Rapporteur ; and three Palestinian human rights organisations . These measures aim to undermine the Rome Statute system as a whole and to prevent the investigation and prosecution of international crimes. Executive Order 14203 prohibits US persons from providing material support or services to designated persons and entities, including financial services, and exposes non-US persons to the risk of secondary sanctions for engaging in conduct prohibited under the Executive Order. US persons who violate it may face criminal penalties of up to 20 years’ imprisonment and fines of up to 1 million USD, as well as civil penalties. Although the Executive Order contains a six-month wind-down period and exemptions for certain services, significant risks remain. Given the global reliance on the US financial and IT systems, even non-US service providers, including banks, may stop rendering their services to the ICC out of fear of penalties or reprisals from the US Treasury. This could impact the Court’s ability to maintain a bank account, receive financial contributions from States Parties, make payments, pay staff and maintain essential operations. The Netherlands, as the host country, and all States Parties are responsible for ensuring the ICC can maintain access to services critical to its operations. The Court must be able to continue to carry out its core functions, including investigating alleged crimes; holding hearings; protecting victims and witnesses; and providing legal aid services. For victims, survivors and witnesses in more than a dozen countries under investigation by the Court across the globe, the consequences could be profound. Many have waited years for justice, recounted traumatic experiences and placed their trust in the ICC as a last resort for justice. Any disruption to the ICC’s mandate and operations risks impeding their right to justice. It threatens decades of advances in accountability and justice efforts, leaving victims of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide without a meaningful prospect for accountability, truth and reparations. The sanctions are already undermining justice efforts . The three Palestinian NGOs designated for cooperating with the Court immediately lost access to their bank accounts, funds, IT services and partners, impeding their work. The damage does not end with those targeted; the sanctions have created a chilling effect and impacted freedom of expression and association worldwide. Sanctions on the Court as an institution risk deepening that effect. Ultimately, victims, families of victims, and survivors will pay the highest price. The US, which is not a State Party, is blatantly attacking the world’s only permanent international criminal court through measures that leverage its position within the global financial system. If the 125 States Parties to the Rome Statute allow these attacks to undermine the Court’s ability to function, the consequences would extend far beyond the ICC, threatening the broader rule of law, states’ sovereignty and systems of justice at the national, regional and international levels. Statements of concern and condemnations are no longer a sufficient response to this attack. A coordinated response can no longer be delayed. Three decades ago, States made a promise that no one, no matter how powerful, will be shielded from accountability for international crimes. Victims and survivors have waited decades for a Court capable of delivering justice regardless of power or nationality, and today, the ICC is facing unprecedented pressure precisely because it seeks to apply the law equally. States Parties established the Court and are uniquely placed to safeguard its independence and effectiveness. Failure to respond decisively risks weakening the international justice system they pledged to uphold. selected.headline: Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz | US-Israel war on Iran News
selected.evidence: The IRGC is hitting more ships allegedly part of a shuttle operation to move crude oil beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran. With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz. This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran. Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers. He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks. “You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted. This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks. Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again. His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted. Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz. Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions. But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis. In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers . It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces. Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war. But Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met. Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, said this reflects Tehran’s apparent assessment that it is under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement with the US since its pressure in the Hormuz has a global impact. “The question, however, is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure, given the growing economic costs of the confrontation for Iran itself,” Azizi wrote on X. The system involves very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and smaller vessels coordinating with the US military to load crude oil at Arab ports and use southern corridors near the coast of Oman to exit the strait. Vessels often switch off their transponders and travel at night to minimise the risk of being targeted by the Iranians. After ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, some of the shuttles come back to load more. Multiple vessels were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday, including two outbound tankers and one in anchorage near Oman’s port city of Sohar, where ship-to-ship transfers are allegedly being conducted. Other vessels were targeted by projectiles last week, indicating that attacks have extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz to target the shuttle system. The IRGC has also increasingly driven a narrative that naval mines, believed to have been planted across the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war, pose a serious threat to vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without coordinating with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority. The IRGC said three tankers suffered major damage over the weekend after being struck by mines. It also released footage of one ship ablaze that is said to have been struck by a mine, although the footage did not appear to show a mine going off. The shuttle system has provided Arab national oil companies with a way out of Hormuz via the southern corridor near Oman. Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a London-based senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, said this system has proven highly effective. “Under international maritime law, which underpins 11 billion tonnes of seaborne trade annually, vessels have what’s called the right of transit passage,” Bockmann told Al Jazeera. “So, what Oman has done is allow vessels to go through under international maritime law, but they have had US military assistance.” Tehran says shipping will be disrupted so long as the US continues its choking naval blockade against Iran, which has also stepped up its efforts to counter efforts by Arab states to export oil. At least 15 ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far, according to Winward. “The more effective the route has become in facilitating the transport of oil and gas, the less leverage Iran has over Hormuz, and more attacks we are seeing on vessels that are using that southern corridor,” Bockmann said. Windward’s data shows 31 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily in the final week of September. This was considerably lower than the 138 before the war. Eighty-seven percent of the 45 ships targeted by Iran during the third quarter of 2026 were tankers. Around 47 percent belonged to Gulf Arab energy companies’ national shipping fleets, Windward noted, and 93 percent of the strikes took place in the Strait of Hormuz. selected.headline: Kremlin rejects Ukraine’s offer of a 60-day truce and presidential elections – The Irish Times
selected.evidence: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has blamed Russia for breaking a purported “energy ceasefire” announced by Donald Trump , signalling that Kyiv will continue its strikes unless Moscow halts its attacks. The US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, in a claim that blindsided officials in Kyiv. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskiy said Trump should have come to him to cut a “diesel deal”, adding that Russia had used drones and missiles to strike power and gas facilities across Ukraine overnight. “Immediately after [Trump’s] post, Russia launched a targeted strike ... It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskiy said. “We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same,” he added, including “to sign guarantees” as proof of Ukraine’s commitment. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not comment on Trump’s ceasefire announcement, telling reporters on Monday that “contacts” between Russia and the US “continue”. Peskov rejected Ukraine’s offer of a 60-day truce and presidential elections. He said Moscow was willing to halt attacks only for a day to allow Ukraine to hold elections. “They need 60 days of ceasefire not for elections, but to regroup, heal their wounds and continue the war,” Peskov said. Despite Moscow’s overnight strikes, European diesel prices fell on Monday as traders responded to Trump’s latest effort to drive down fuel prices in the US before November’s midterm elections. His announcement of an “energy ceasefire” came after the US president on Friday struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to release more diesel. The price of diesel – a vital fuel for industry and agriculture – has soared as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine knock out infrastructure and strain global supplies. Speaking in Warsaw, Zelenskiy said: “Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning. But at midnight a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone hit a gas plant in Ukraine ... This is Putin’s answer to Trump.” Parts of Kyiv and other cities across Ukraine were plunged into darkness on Sunday night into Monday morning following the Russian strikes. Water was knocked out in much of the Ukrainian capital. Russian drones continued to attack Kyiv on Monday after Zelenskiy’s conference speech, with heavy air-defence fire and explosions reverberating throughout the city. Sergii Fedorenko, acting chief executive of Ukraine’s state gas company Naftogaz, said critical equipment was damaged by a Russian jet-powered drone. Vitaliy Bunechko, the governor of Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, said Russian drones had struck energy and railway facilities there. Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum he did not believe the volume of diesel Russia would export as part of Trump’s deal would affect the price. “Moreover, we see they can export from 300,000 to 500,000 tonnes a month today. Meanwhile, global consumption stands at 120 million tonnes a month,” he said. “What kind of impact can that have? I don’t think it would have any.” “If some people think otherwise, so be it,” he said in an apparent reference to Trump. “If this is the approach, then why isn’t America making a ‘diesel deal’ with Ukraine? Let Ukraine propose a ‘diesel deal’.” Ukraine, Zelenskiy said, through its long-range drones that have attacked Russian oil and gas facilities and shadow fleet ships, had “influence over whether these ships can sail or not, whether these refineries can operate or not”. He added: “If that’s the case, then let’s do it.” The Trump administration had also threatened to stop the procurement system that provided Ukraine with weapons to pressure Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, officials told the Financial Times. That followed a warning on Friday from the Trump administration to Zelenskiy’s peace negotiators in Miami that Washington could cut off vital intelligence sharing with Kyiv unless it halts the air attacks against Russian oil refineries. “We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians,” Zelenskiy said. “Putin is so shamelessly trying to sell his refineries to the world as a solution.” EU foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Monday agreed to impose sanctions against about 1,600 additional individuals and entities from Russia’s military-industrial complex. “If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat. “We would call on US to put the sanctions in place so that actually we could finish this war and all these effects of attacks on refineries would not be there.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026 [ Daniel McLaughlin: Ukraine backs Trump's energy ceasefire, but is Russia on board? selected.evidence: Two commercial vessels were attacked near Oman on Sunday, two Indian sailors were left missing, and a drone struck an Iranian Kurdish opposition camp in Iraq on Monday, as Iranian officials warned that a renewed war could put regional infrastructure at risk. Separately, the Marshall Islands-flagged Valthera was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, setting off a fire onboard; all 11 Indian crew members were safe, India’s foreign ministry said. The ministry condemned the attacks, and India’s embassy in Muscat was coordinating with Omani authorities to help locate the missing sailors. The latest incidents followed repeated attacks on commercial vessels in the region, but the statements from India did not identify who was responsible for Sunday’s strikes. Separately, a drone struck a camp belonging to an Iranian Kurdish opposition group in Koya, east of Erbil in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, Reuters reported, citing two security sources. No casualties were immediately reported. Kurdistan-based website Rudaw published video showing a drone in the sky over Koya, but said it was not yet clear whether it had hit a target. No responsibility for the reported strike was established. The incidents came as Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned that a renewed war could put infrastructure across the region within range. “If war breaks out, many cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities, valued at $2 trillion, will be within range,” he said, according to state media. Rezaei added that Iran would continue resisting until its adversaries accepted its rights. Iranian officials also continued to issue warnings to Washington and regional governments. Acting Defense Minister Majid Ebn al-Reza said the armed forces were ready to respond to threats and urged neighboring countries to leave what he called the US security umbrella. His remarks followed a statement by armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi that Iran would not allow the United States and Israel to re-establish their preferred regional order. At the same time, diplomatic contacts had not stopped. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran was reviewing Washington’s latest proposal and that messages between the two countries continued through mediators. Baghaei gave no indication of a breakthrough, saying Iran’s position on the Strait of Hormuz remained tied to the US naval blockade. The developments pointed to risks spreading across shipping routes, Iraqi Kurdistan and potentially digital infrastructure, even as intermediaries continued trying to keep US-Iran diplomacy alive. Efforts to end the war with Iran and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained deadlocked Sunday, as military pressure continued at sea and the Iran-backed Houthis carried out increasingly deadly attacks inside Saudi Arabia. Iran said the United States had accepted some of seven conditions it presented for reopening the strait but that Washington's response was insufficient, leaving the two sides without agreement on renewed negotiations or unrestricted passage through the waterway. “The US has agreed to some of Iran’s seven conditions, but we consider its response INADEQUATE,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said in a post on X. “Iranian diplomacy has changed and there will be no return to the status quo ante.” Iran presented the seven-condition proposal during the UN General Assembly, offering to restore normal maritime passage through the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if its conditions were met. The United States later responded through Qatari intermediaries. The latest exchange comes days after Axios reported that the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command to complete preparations for the possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran. President Donald Trump subsequently said the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and described talks with Tehran as “productive.” Rezaei, however, said Washington still needed to clarify parts of its response and that Iran would not reopen the strait to the United States or resume negotiations until its conditions were met. Iran, for its part, has continued restricting passage through the strait. The IRGC Navy said Sunday that a tanker carrying 750,000 barrels of crude struck a naval mine and caught fire after attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route despite warnings. The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency described it as the third tanker to strike a mine in the strait that day. The incidents come amid a sharp deterioration in shipping security this month. Seven of the vessels attacked in the strait sustained only minor damage and continued their transit, UKMTO said. Vessel traffic through Hormuz remained about 75% below pre-conflict levels. According to BFM TV, France’s largest supermarket chain E Leclerc was also affected, with hackers “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. E Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment. The attack may not have been confined to France. The Dutch supermarket company ‌Ahold Delhaize said it was also dealing with a “security issue” in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them. Stores of its Albert Heijn chain, ​the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, which also has several stores in Belgium, remained open in both countries. But its online app and delivery system were down, while electronic price tags often displayed the wrong information. It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the ⁠problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize. Delhaize supermarkets, also part of Ahold Delhaize but operating ​in Belgium and Luxembourg, were ​also affected by the security issue, ​Belgian media reported. The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability ​in software supplied by ‌the Danish company Danfoss. selected.headline: NATO commander says the alliance does not want war but is 'ready to fight tonight'
selected.evidence: Emma Burrows, Associated Press Emma Burrows, Associated Press WARSAW, Poland (AP) — NATO's top military commander said the alliance is "ready to fight tonight" if it is attacked, as European officials warn Russia could test NATO's defenses with increased covert attacks or a limited military incursion. European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport. If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S. General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw Monday. Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called NATO's "Theory of Victory." The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings." Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack NATO is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces. But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said NATO's combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground. "My theory of victory is simple," he told the Warsaw conference. "We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us." That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said. In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the NATO alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent. Denmark's defense intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the NATO alliance. But, at the same time, President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try lower prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections. WATCH: Poland braces for potential confrontation as Russia tests NATO defenses Earlier this year, the U.S. president said he was pulling American troops from Europe and his war with Iran has led to critical shortages of advanced air defense missiles in Europe. "Ultimately it's a political decision," as to where troops are deployed but "no one should question the U.S. commitment to the alliance," Grynkewich said. It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a "coherent" response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow "where our red lines are." The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine. While Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning to escalate with drone or rocket strikes on European allies supporting Ukraine, other countries have called for calm. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Agency said there is a "low but growing risk" that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia. NATO does not seek war with anyone but will see a military attack coming and "is unlikely to be caught by surprise," Grynkewich said. Although Grynkewich said NATO would defend against any attack by Russia using a network of sensors and autonomous systems, some NATO nations have previously struggled to perform in exercises simulating drone warfare. They have also faced challenges detecting and responding to incursions of drones which have entered their airspace. Multiple attack drones have crashed in NATO countries bordering Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. And in May, residents in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius were told to seek shelter after a drone strayed into Lithuanian airspace. When asked if NATO could deter Russia in the way Grynkewich described, his spokesperson, Col. Martin O'Donnell said NATO nations are increasingly deploying ground sensors and other technology to detect and counter drones. The network that connects systems to shoot down drones and sensors is in the process of being established, although they have not yet taken down any drones, he said. In September, Germany accused Russia of being behind a plot at Leipzig airport to use a drone laden with explosives to attack a Ukrainian aircraft. British officials also said they thwarted a Russian plot to target a drone facility outside London while Estonian officials said Russia was behind a fire at a defense company. The incidents are among at least 211 blamed on Russia by Western officials since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and tracked by The Associated Press. In its assessment released earlier in September, Denmark's defense intelligence service suggested Russia could try to acquire Ukrainian drones and use them to attack Europe, in order to obfuscate any Russian involvement. Tusk suggested Russia will likely pretend any attacks are "accidental" in order to "paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries" to rush to the defense of a member state coming under attack. The Danish service said the aim of any such attack would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine and sow division in NATO. But both the Danish service and O'Donnell said while Russia is fighting in Ukraine, it would be difficult to launch an outright attack on NATO. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. selected.headline: Bangladesh, WB, IMF reach policy consensus on reforms, govt focuses on investment | The Business Standard
selected.evidence: Adviser to the Prime Minister on Finance and Planning Prof Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir today (12 October) said Bangladesh has reached broad policy alignment with the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on key economic reforms aimed at restoring stability, strengthening discipline in the banking sector, increasing tax revenue and creating employment. "The government is pursuing a comprehensive economic recovery and reconstruction strategy, with greater domestic and foreign investment, reopening closed factories, expanding social protection and addressing rising energy costs among its major priorities," he said. The adviser made the remarks while speaking to journalists ahead of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Thailand, said a press release. Titumir said the government had a politically mandated roadmap to recover, restore and rapidly rebuild the economy to put the country on a path to prosperity. The plan has been outlined in a five-year economic strategy, with several fundamental priorities aligning with the reform proposals of the World Bank and the IMF, he added. "The people want discipline in the financial sector, higher tax collection relative to GDP, increased spending on social protection and employment generation through industrialisation," he said, adding that reopening closed factories was also a public expectation. The adviser said alignment between the government's reform priorities and those of multilateral development partners would facilitate implementation and improve the prospects for sustainable reforms. However, he emphasised that the political government would retain ownership of the reform agenda and responsibility for its implementation. Titumir said the government had discussed with the World Bank the additional financial pressure on the energy sector arising from the conflict in the Middle East, which began on 28 February, and its impact on ordinary people. He said the government had refrained from fully adjusting domestic energy prices to international market levels to limit the burden on consumers. Referring to the World Bank's recent report, he said poverty had increased during the previous government's tenure. The present government is planning to support poor households through programmes such as the Family Card, he added. According to assessments by independent research institutions, such initiatives could potentially reduce the poverty rate by around five percentage points over five years, he said. The government has also highlighted the need for financing to strengthen climate resilience, expand renewable energy and develop essential infrastructure. Titumir identified restoring discipline in the financial sector as one of the major challenges to economic recovery. He said ordinary citizens were now bearing the consequences of irregularities and lending-related disorder in the banking sector during the previous administration. Restoring confidence in banks and rehabilitating the weakened financial system would require refinancing support, he said, adding that discussions were underway with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and other institutions on the issue. Without stability in the banking sector, it would be difficult to achieve the targets for higher investment and employment, he continued. The adviser also stressed the need to raise the tax-to-GDP ratio, saying excessive tax exemptions and irregularities in tax administration had weakened revenue collection in the past. Lower revenue mobilisation had widened the fiscal deficit and constrained public spending on social protection and development, he said. He called for coordinated action to strengthen financial discipline, increase revenue, expand social safety nets and create jobs. The government is taking initiatives to arrange special financing to reopen closed factories and encourage fresh investment, Titumir said. He noted that the number of educated and young unemployed people was growing while many factories remained shut, requiring coordinated efforts to boost production, develop new entrepreneurs and generate employment. Migrant workers, entrepreneurs in the ready-made garment sector and women's participation in formal employment had played important roles in Bangladesh's economic progress, he said. The country would need to build on these contributions by expanding production and employment opportunities alongside social protection programmes, he added. He said several promising sectors for Thai investment in Bangladesh had been highlighted during a meeting with the Thai Chamber of Commerce, particularly those offering opportunities for production, processing and value addition. selected.headline: B.C. man reunited with beloved flute, 5 years after it floated away down a Yukon river
selected.evidence: Jun Takahashi was stunned when he saw the post on social media. "Like, what? Like, I couldn't believe it," he said, from his home on Salt Spring Island, B.C. The post on a Yukon paddling group page was by someone who had recently found a blue, waterproof canoe barrel full of camping gear, near the confluence of a couple of remote Yukon rivers. The poster, Colin Abbott, asked if anybody had dumped in Yukon's Kathleen River "in the last couple of years" and might be missing their gear. There was also a picture, showing the blue barrel, some clothes and a sleeping bag strewn across a floor — and, in the middle, a flute in a case. Colin Abbott posted this photo on social media after he found the barrel full of gear last month. (Colin Abbott) Takahashi recognized it immediately. The flute meant a lot to him — he'd bought in Japan years ago and had carried it with him on his many travels. It was the perfect thing to travel with, especially on a remote canoe trip in the Yukon. It could be easily stuffed inside one of those waterproof barrels for your gear. Takahashi also loved to play it in wild, open spaces. Takahashi likes to play his flute in remote places where he won't disturb anyone. (Submitted by Jun Takahashi) Before last week, he'd assumed he would never see the instrument again. He lost it in June 2021, when he and a friend were on a canoe trip down the Kathleen River and accidentally flipped their boat. It was a scramble to escape the frigid water with their lives, so the canoe and their gear had to be left to be swept down the fast-moving river. In the following days, the two took to social media asking any paddlers to keep an eye out for their gear and even offered a cash reward. Takahashi and Sonia Lévêque on their ill-fated canoe trip in 2021. (Submitted by Jun Takahashi) Takahashi thought the lost barrel might be adrift somewhere on the Bering Sea by now. Or, he imagined an "Alaskan bear wearing my down jacket or like, playing my flute or something." It turns out the barrel, and all of its contents, had not travelled that far. selected.headline: Moments after Houthi strike, Bangladeshi pilgrim tried to reach family one last time
selected.evidence: DHAKA: Moments after a Houthi strike hit the Riyadh airport where he was transiting, Nasrullah Badar called his family in Dhaka but could not utter a word. A day later, his brother learned he did not survive the attack. A 37-year-old teacher and imam, Badar was leading a group of 44 Bangladeshis on their Umrah pilgrimage. They left Dhaka on Saturday morning and were waiting two hours at King Khalid International Airport for another flight to Jeddah. At that time, in the early afternoon, the Houthi missile hit the site. “At the time of the attack, they were about to board the plane. The explosion occurred right beside him, as I heard from other pilgrims,” his elder brother, Mohammad Ahsan Ullah Badar, told Arab News. “After the explosion, he called us twice. Although we received the call, we couldn’t hear his voice. Probably due to severe injury, he couldn’t utter a word. Later, we called back again, and again. But the calls went unanswered.” In the evening, the number was no longer reachable. “For an entire day, we found no trace of him. We searched in various hospitals, everywhere, but found nothing,” the brother said. “One day later, on Sunday at 4 p.m., we received the tragic news through the Bangladeshi Embassy in Saudi Arabia.” Badar was one of two Bangladeshis among 13 people killed in Saturday’s missile attack on the Saudi capital. More than 300 others were injured, including 24 from Bangladesh. They are 11 migrant workers and 13 Umrah pilgrims and remain hospitalized, according to Dhaka’s embassy in Riyadh. Badar leaves behind two little sons and a daughter. When he landed in Riyadh, he called his wife and parents. “While talking with our father, he said he wished to perform Umrah on his behalf ... He also asked our mother to pray for him,” Badar’s brother said. “My younger brother Nasrullah Badar was a very nice and kind-hearted person. The government has transferred the unused machinery from the Sonali Bag project to Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University (MBSTU) to prevent public assets from deteriorating and support further research into jute-based products and technologies. A memorandum of understanding was signed on October 8 among the Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation (BJMC), the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust and the university. State Minister for Textiles and Jute Shariful Alam handed over the machinery to the university’s vice-chancellor. The move comes after the much-anticipated Sonali Bag -- a biodegradable alternative to plastic, made from jute cellulose -- failed to become commercially viable. According to a BJMC statement sent to The Daily Star, the Tk 100 crore project was scrapped on April 29, 2025, following a technical committee’s recommendation. The 11-member committee found that producing five tonnes of Sonali bags required 40 tonnes of chemicals, raising environmental concerns. Each bag would need to sell for Tk 25-40 to cover production costs, making it commercially unviable, the statement said. Talking to The Daily Star, Shariful Alam said the government is working with the environment ministry and other institutions to develop environmentally friendly alternatives to polythene bags. Although the project had made technological progress, production costs could not be reduced to commercially acceptable levels, he said. The state minister said the machinery will support research into jute cellulose, eco-friendly products and new technologies. Private researchers will also be able to access the facilities, while the ministry may use them for research and training. Shariful Alam said reusable jute bags could offer long-term savings despite their higher initial cost. Dr Mubarak Ahmed Khan, who invented the Sonali Bag in 2016, said the project stalled because the government did not provide the necessary funding. He subsequently left the project, he said. Questioning the production-cost estimate, Khan said a feasibility study put the cost at Tk 500 per kilogramme, but he did not know how the figure had been calculated. He argued that costs would fall as production increased and said he had presented his own calculations to officials. Several local and foreign companies have since expressed interest in the technology, he said. “Different private companies, both local and foreign, want to take it forward. The Sonali Bag factory was established at Latif Bawany Jute Mills in Demra in 2019 with Tk 10 crore from the Bangladesh Climate Trust Fund. Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists. Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names. Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution. "We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi. Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi. Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests. Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists." Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen. The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July. JAKARTA — Indonesia says it no longer needs to expand rice cultivation into forest areas, but it has yet to explain what the announcement means for large-scale food and energy projects already underway in Papua and Kalimantan. Presidential Special Envoy for Climate and Energy Hashim Djojohadikusumo said Oct. 6 that Indonesia had achieved rice self-sufficiency three years ahead of schedule and no longer needed the previously announced 2 million hectares (4.9 million acres) for food production. “The government sees no further need for expanding rice cultivation areas in the so-called forest areas and forest zones that were announced a few years ago,” Hashim said in Jakarta. At the same event, President’s Special Envoy for Multilateralism and International Trade Mari Pangestu said future food and biofuel production would instead be directed toward degraded land. The announcement appears to mark a shift from a government push that environmentalists have described as one of the world’s largest deforestation projects , involving vast rice and sugarcane plantations in southern Papua. But less than two weeks before Hashim’s announcement, the Ministry of Forestry designated about 5.67 million hectares (14 million acres) of forest through its 2026 Forest Utilization Direction Map, or PAPH, as areas that could be proposed for forest-utilization permits, including for food security and energy, as well as forest rehabilitation. “This means there is an inconsistency between the statements issued by public officials,” Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi) campaigner for essential ecosystems Musdalifah Jamal told Mongabay by phone. “This contradiction shows us that the government has not yet abandoned a development paradigm that places forest areas as spaces to fulfill food and energy needs.” The forestry ministry has welcomed the direction of Hashim’s announcement but has not said whether it changes existing policies or projects. “A distinction needs to be made between new expansion plans that require the clearing of forest areas, activities that are already under way, and increasing production on agricultural land that is already available,” ministry spokesperson Ristianto Pribadi said, as quoted by The Straits Times . “Therefore, we cannot yet say that all activities in the two regions will automatically stop, nor confirm when they will stop,” he said, referring to South Papua and Central Kalimantan. Environmental groups say the announcement must therefore be followed by changes to policies that have facilitated forest conversion. “At face value, the statements from Pak Hashim and Ibu Mari Pangestu said the Government of Indonesia would no longer pursue deforestation for food or energy crops,” Mighty Earth founder and CEO Glenn Hurowitz told Mongabay. “In order for these positive statements to have impact, they have to be implemented, including by changes in decrees and other policies.” Nadia Hadad, executive director of NGO MADANI Berkelanjutan, said the government also needs to align its food, energy, forestry and fiscal policies with the new commitment. “Climate commitments are ultimately not measured by how many statements are made, but by whether policies and state money move in the same direction,” she said in a press release. Franky Samperante, director of the Pusaka Foundation, which works with Indigenous peoples in Papua, said officials often express commitments to sustainable development and forest protection that have yet to be translated into concrete policies and actions. Corporate heavy machinery is still clearing natural forests in several areas of Papua targeted for food estate programs, including rice fields, sugarcane plantations and oil-palm plantations, he said. Indigenous communities, who are custodians of the land and forests, have also faced alleged harassment and criminalization, prompting United Nations rights officials to raise concerns over alleged human rights abuses and environmental destruction linked to the project. Dressed in black, Taghiyev stands in the centre among the pupils and teachers of the Baku Muslim Girls’ School. New school uniform requirements have once again brought Azerbaijan’s secular tradition into conflict with the religious beliefs of some families. But behind the dispute over clothing lies a simpler question: how can every girl be kept in education? In videos shared on social media, schoolgirls wearing headscarves leave school in tears: they have been denied entry to lessons. The voices of the pupils themselves are heard far less often in the public debate than declarations about their future. A headscarf alone cannot reveal whether a girl wears it out of personal conviction, family custom or pressure. Nor can her tears establish every cause of the conflict. That is why any solution must begin with a conversation with the child, rather than assigning someone else’s position to her. For some parents, what is happening has already become a question of access to education. One parent in Sumgayit told AzadlıqRadiosu : “Our children are not being allowed into school because of our religious beliefs.” This is a parent’s testimony, rather than a fact established by a court. But it identifies these families’ central fear: a clothing requirement could mean missed lessons. The current dispute gained fresh momentum following Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309 of September 21, 2026. It added a prohibition to the school uniform rules on clothing elements that undermine the uniform’s consistency and do not comply with the principle of secular general education. Yet the word “hijab” does not appear in the document. Questions of compliance have been assigned to schools’ pedagogical councils , while parents are required to ensure that their children follow the rules. National dress, or elements of it, may be worn at events dedicated to Azerbaijan’s history and culture with the permission of the pedagogical council. The distinction between the resolution’s wording and its practical application matters. The document establishes clothing requirements, but contains no explicit provision barring pupils from lessons specifically for wearing hijab. Each such case therefore requires separate examination: who made the decision, on what grounds, in what form, and how can the family appeal? The official position of education authorities centres on order and equality. Announcing checks on uniform compliance, the Baku City Education Department said the aim was to create a disciplined, orderly and equal educational environment. School management is responsible for oversight, while disputed questions are referred to pedagogical councils. There is an understandable educational logic to this position. A common uniform can reduce displays of economic differences, simplify school rules and reinforce a sense of belonging to the same community. But a question remains: if the rest of a pupil’s clothing meets the prescribed uniform requirements, must a headscarf be prohibited to achieve those goals? There is no single interpretation within the education community. In comments to Referans Media , education expert Elchin Efendi stresses the need to comply with school uniform requirements and prevent religious views from being imposed on other pupils. His colleague Ramin Nuraliyev points to the absence of an explicit ban on covering the head. “A girl wearing a headscarf does not mean a departure from the school uniform,” he told AzEdu. An important distinction lies here: personal religious expression and pressure on others require different assessments. Appearance alone does not prove an attempt to impose beliefs. In Azerbaijan, a dispute over women’s head coverings inevitably becomes a conversation about history. Some see contemporary hijab as a return to religious practice; others see the spread of clothing that differs from the familiar appearance of mothers and grandmothers. A historical distinction exists, but it is difficult to capture in the formula “there was no hijab before”. Hijab does not denote one unchanging style of clothing. In contemporary everyday speech, the word often refers to a scarf covering the hair and neck; in broader religious usage, it refers to standards for covering the body. The kelaghayi, an ordinary headscarf and the chador are specific garments that could carry cultural, practical and religious significance at the same time. Azerbaijani tradition was diverse. The national portal describes kelaghayi, other scarves and head coverings , their combinations and regional characteristics. Sometimes the hair was first gathered beneath one covering, with a silk scarf tied over it. Fabrics, patterns and ways of wearing them varied. The observation that younger women wore brightly coloured scarves and older women darker ones is reflected in materials from Azerbaijan’s National Commission for UNESCO . But colour also depended on the occasion: a wedding, mourning, a celebration or everyday life. UNESCO, which added the art of making and wearing kelaghayi to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2014, links the tradition to both cultural identity and religious customs. The chador, also called a charshab, differed from a headscarf: it was a larger covering that concealed the head and much of the body. Photographs and paintings from the 19th and early 20th centuries therefore need to be read carefully. Urban clothing could differ from rural dress, festive clothing from everyday attire, and the costume of one locality from that of another. These images testify to the diversity of the past. They do not justify declaring a single way of dressing the compulsory expression of national identity. The emancipation of Azerbaijani women cannot be reduced to the moment when the chador was removed

selected.headline: The building blocks of life on Earth have been found around distant stars that are similar to our Solar System | BBC Sky at Night Magazine
selected.evidence: Discovery suggests raw ingredients for life are common in the dusty discs out of which planets are born. The materials that form the building blocks of life on Earth have been found in distant planet-forming discs that are the same size as the Solar System. Our Solar System formed from a dusty ring of cosmic material circling the Sun , when our host star was still just a stellar newborn. This ring - known as a protoplanetary disk - contained solid materials that coalesced through gravity over time, eventually growing into the the planets orbiting the Sun that we see today. Studying other young stars and their protoplanetary discs enables astronomers to analyse the conditions that may have led to the formation of of our own Solar System, and perhaps even the development of life on Earth. Dr John Ilee is an astrophysicist studying star and planet formation at the University of Leeds. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, he and his colleagues have identified organic molecules in protoplanetary discs around young stars, which could point to the building blocks required for the development of organic life. These discs are located between about 300 to 500 lightyears from Earth, so we are actually seeing the discs as they appeared 300 to 500 years ago. The regions in which these discs exist are some of the closest star-forming regions to our Solar System, which means we can get an excellent view of them. Compared to previous instruments, ALMA has hugely increased our observational capability. It combines extremely high sensitivity with a high spatial resolution. This means we can detect faint emission on small scales, which was essential for our study. We searched for the unique ‘fingerprints’ of these molecules in the ALMA data, which were very faint, but thanks to the data’s exceptional quality we were able to detect their emission. These molecules have been detected in protoplanetary discs before, but the fact that we’ve been able to get such improved observations means the abundance of these molecules is much higher than previously thought. Additionally, they’re located in the ‘inner’ disc regions, within about 50 astronomical units, which is approximately the same scale as our Solar System. This means we are finding significant amounts of prebiotic materials (which form the building blocks of life) on similar scales to a planetary system like our own. The findings suggest that the chemical composition of discs that appear to be forming planets is similar to the composition of our own Solar System. However, we don’t know if this is required to form planets. To investigate this we’d need to study the composition of a much larger and statistically significant sample of protoplanetary discs. This is something that ALMA will be able to do in the near future. Complex organic molecules are found in various environments throughout space, such as the giant clouds of gas and dust that will eventually go on to form stars. Studies have suggested that molecules such as these are the ‘raw ingredients’ for building molecules that are essential components in biological chemistry on Earth – including things like sugars and the bases of ribonucleic acid (RNA). However, many of the environments where we find these complex organic molecules are pretty far removed from where we think planets form. We wanted to understand more about where and how much of these molecules were present in the birthplaces of planets – protoplanetary discs. While we can’t say that for certain, the take-home message is that we find these ‘prebiotic’ molecules in large abundances, and at distances from their parent star that are similar in size to our Solar System. So that suggests the raw ingredients for life are plentiful in the disc of material that forms planets. Three of the discs in our sample are around T Tauri stars, which are younger versions of stars that are similar to our Sun. These three objects represent a young stellar evolutionary stage that may go on to form a planetary system similar to our own. We want to know how the molecules got there. Had they been formed in situ by chemical reactions in the disc? Or have they been inherited from the earlier star-forming phase when the disc was assembled from a large cloud of gas and dust? Answering these questions would be one of our next steps.

Astronomers investigating mysterious flashes of X-rays believe that these blasts could stem from collisions between neutron stars, the events that forge elements like gold, silver, and platinum. The event designated EP250704a, was first seen on July 4, 2025, as a blast of gamma rays lasting half a second followed by a bright X-ray emission lasting 10 minutes. After receiving an alert from the joint European-Chinese Einstein probe that witnessed the blast, a team of astronomers started to hunt for its cause by studying the aftermath of the explosion using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Very Large Array (VLA), and other telescopes. According to astronomer Niccolò Passaleva who led the observations of the X-ray flash with the VLT, this cosmic outburst was unlike any scientists had seen before. "This is the longest-lasting prompt X-ray flash ever observed from a neutron star merger," Passaleva said in a statement . "It is an opportunity to have a front-row seat to the most extreme forces of the universe and discover more of its secrets." Neutron stars are created when massive stars die in supernova explosions, cramming one or two the mass of the sun into a width akin to a city on Earth and creating material so dense that a single teaspoon of neutron star matter brought to Earth would weigh 10 million tons. When these extreme dead stars slam together, they create environments so turbulent and violent they are capable of forging elements so heavy that even the hearts of stars can't do it. Elements like the gold on your finger. These collision and merger events, marked by flashes of light called kilonovas , have long been associated with flashes of high-energy gamma-rays that disappear within two seconds, but new research suggests some neutron star mergers could reveal themselves via blasts of X-rays lasting minutes. In particular, scientists have wondered if neutron star mergers could be the cause of hundreds of X-ray flashes in distant galaxies discovered by the Einstein probe since its launch in 2024. While some of these have been linked to the supernova-explosive death of massive stars that can create a neutron star or a black hole , others have defied explanation. EP250704a is one such X-ray flash. "When I saw the X-ray data from this new event, I realized something was up," team member Eleonora Troja, part of the Einstein Probe European collaboration, said in the statement. The team believes that there is something special in the neutron star merger mix that results in these X-ray bursts. All neutron stars are created the same way from the collapsing core of a massive star, but not all neutron stars are equal. Just as an ice skater pulls in their arms to increase the speed of a spin, the rapid reduction in radius of a collapsing stellar core can "spin up" the rotation of a neutron star to 'over 700 times per second. This collapse can have another consequence too. It turns out that magnetic fields get stronger when magnetic field lines are pushed closer together. That means the collapse of a stellar core with an already powerful magnetic field can create a neutron star with the strongest magnetic field in the universe. Those neutron stars have a special name: magnetars . The team behind this research thinks that the neutron star merger in question involved at least one magnetar. "If the remnant of the collision is a magnetar, it could keep bursting for longer," Troja said. "Magnetars are rapidly spinning neutron stars with huge magnetic fields. When they dump their magnetic power into the surroundings, they can make any explosion brighter and longer-lasting." The researchers ruled out a supernova as the cause of the X-ray burst and were also able to determine that the light from this collision has been travelling to Earth for 6 billion years. Discovering more of these extreme X-ray flashes could help astronomers determine how often magnetars are formed through these neutron star mergers, Passaleva said in the statement. The team's research was published in the journal Science Bulletin. selected.headline: New Jurassic crocodile species had unusually slender teeth, suggesting it fed on shrimp and tiny fish
selected.evidence: edited by Swati Mestri , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: A new species of ancient crocodile relative that lived around 170 million years ago has been discovered by scientists at the University of Portsmouth and Hassan II University of Casablanca, Morocco. Unlike most crocodiles, this animal had a long, narrow snout filled with exceptionally thin, needlelike teeth. The teeth were so slender that they are unlike those of any known close relative. The animal, named Ctenosuchus tenuidens, belonged to a group of marine and freshwater reptiles known as thalattosuchians, which lived during the age of the dinosaurs. The fossils were found in rocks that formed in ancient rivers and lakes in what is now the Atlas Mountains of southeastern Morocco. Hamzah Imran from the University of Portsmouth's School of the Environment and Life Sciences is lead author of the research published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology . He said, "We noticed these little black circles on either side of the long bone in the middle of one of the fossils, so we put it under a microscope. "We carefully scratched around one of the black circles with a scalpel, and as we uncovered more of it, it became longer and longer. That's when we realized these little black circles were actually incredibly thin teeth. "These comblike teeth inspired the name Ctenosuchus tenuidens, as 'cteno' means 'comb,' 'suchus' means 'crocodile,' and 'tenuidens' means 'thin teeth.'" By studying the fossil teeth under powerful microscopes and examining their internal structure, Imran and his colleagues found that the teeth had specialized ridges and were closely spaced. These features suggest that Ctenosuchus had a very unusual diet. Rather than hunting large prey, it likely fed on very small fish, crustaceans such as fairy shrimp and other small aquatic creatures. Imran said, "The teeth are so fine that we don't think it was catching normal prey. If it caught a big fish, and the fish wriggled, those delicate teeth would get smashed. We think the animal was probably eating soft prey like shrimp, worms and tiny fish, so nothing that would break its teeth. "These feeding habits make this particular species very different from other long-snouted crocodiles, so it really is quite an exciting discovery!" The research helps scientists better understand the diversity and ecology of ancient crocodile relatives that lived in the southern supercontinent Gondwana, which included modern-day Africa. It also shows that different groups of prehistoric animals evolved similar feeding adaptations independently. The teeth of Ctenosuchus resemble those seen in some ancient aquatic reptiles called mesosaurs and even certain long-snouted pterosaurs that lived millions of years later. In fact, the jaws and teeth of Ctenosuchus have many similarities with the jaws of some Jurassic pterosaurs such as Gnathosaurus and Ctenochasma that scientists believe were filter feeders. Overall, the fossils reveal that Jurassic crocodile relatives occupied a wider range of habitats and feeding roles than previously realized, highlighting the rich prehistoric ecosystems that once existed in Morocco. Imran added, "It just shows there is much more out there that needs to be explored. Morocco has an incredibly rich fossil history, but there is still so much waiting to be discovered."
