selected.headline: Brain entropy during a psychedelic trip tracks later gains in insight and well-being
selected.evidence: A single high dose of psilocybin in people who had never taken a psychedelic was followed by improvements in well-being, psychological insight, and cognitive flexibility a month later, and participants whose brain activity became more irregular during the experience tended to show the largest well-being gains. Lasting changes in brain function, however, were largely absent, though the researchers detected possible changes in the brain’s white matter. The findings were published in Nature Communications . Psilocybin is the active psychedelic compound found in “magic mushrooms.” It works primarily by stimulating a specific type of serotonin receptor in the brain. Some scientists have proposed that this chemical action scrambles normal brain activity into a more flexible, highly disordered state. For instance, a 2014 theoretical paper by Robin Carhart-Harris, the senior author of the new study, introduced the “entropic brain” hypothesis, suggesting that psychedelics expand conscious experience by making brain signals more unpredictable. Researchers have suspected that this temporary disruption might lead to lasting benefits. Along these lines, a 2021 open-label study of 24 people with depression found that psilocybin improved cognitive flexibility for at least a month. Cognitive flexibility is a person’s ability to successfully adapt their thinking and switch between different rules or concepts. Scientists then began tracking healthy volunteers for weeks after a single dose to see whether these acute disruptions leave enduring functional or physical marks on the brain. For example, a small 2020 study of 12 healthy volunteers found that some changes in mood and resting brain connectivity were still detectable a month after a single high dose, although others had faded. Similarly, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that psilocybin temporarily scrambled brain network connections, with most changes fading within weeks but some, such as reduced connectivity between the hippocampus and a network involved in self-reflection, persisting. Building on this progression, the current research, led by Taylor Lyons of the Centre for Psychedelic Research at Imperial College London, sought to capture a comprehensive picture of what happens in the brain of someone taking a psychedelic for the very first time. The researchers aimed to connect the immediate, disorganized brain state during a trip to the psychological benefits reported weeks later. They also wanted to test whether a single high dose of psilocybin physically alters the structure of the brain’s white matter. The study involved 28 healthy adults, averaging 41 years old, who had never taken a psychedelic drug before. Each participant received two oral doses of psilocybin one month apart, always in the same order: first a 1-milligram dose, too low to produce noticeable psychedelic effects, which served as a placebo, and then a 25-milligram high dose known to induce a profound altered state of consciousness. The researchers used this fixed order because they expected the high dose to have lasting effects that could carry over into a later session. To limit expectations, participants were told only that they would receive a variable dose of up to 25 milligrams at each session. Both dosing sessions took place in a supportive environment featuring low lighting, music, an eye mask, and non-directive guided supervision. During dosing days, the research team recorded electrical brain activity using an electroencephalogram, or EEG, while participants rested with their eyes closed at one, two, and four and a half hours after ingestion. Participants also completed magnetic resonance imaging brain scans before the study began and one month after each dose. During the high-dose session, the EEG recordings showed large increases in brain entropy, meaning the electrical signals became highly irregular and unpredictable. This peak in disorganized activity occurred one to two hours after taking the 25-milligram pill, aligning with the peak intensity of the psychedelic experience. The recordings also showed a drop in alpha waves, a rhythm of electrical activity common when people are awake and relaxed, while the 1-milligram placebo dose produced no such changes. When asked months later, all but one of the participants who answered (94 percent) rated the high dose as the most unusual state of consciousness of their lives. When analyzing the brain scans taken a month after the high dose, the researchers found possible changes in the brain’s white matter, the bundles of insulated nerve fibers that carry signals between brain regions. Using a technique called diffusion tensor imaging, which maps how water moves along these fiber pathways, they observed a decrease in water diffusion along tracts connecting the prefrontal cortex to deeper subcortical regions. The prefrontal cortex is involved in complex thinking and decision-making, and this alteration was not observed following the placebo dose. Other brain imaging measures showed little lasting change. Functional MRI scans, which track blood flow as a proxy for brain activity and which the researchers had designated as their primary outcome, revealed changes one month after the high dose that were largely weak and not statistically significant. One measure, network modularity, reflects how sharply the brain divides into separate, tightly knit networks; it decreased compared with the start of the study but not compared with the month after the placebo dose, and participants with larger decreases tended to show larger gains in well-being. An earlier analysis of the same participants’ brain scans, covered by PsyPost in 2026 , focused on circuits linking the prefrontal cortex with the striatum and thalamus, the same pathways where the white matter changes appeared. Using a different analytic approach, it found that activity in these circuits became more variable a month after the high dose than after the placebo dose
